evidence: src/business/services/PayrollService.ts: constructor injects EmployeeRepository and TimesheetRepository; uses this.timesheets.create/approve/forWeek and this.employees.byId/active, then builds Employee/Timesheet model objects
src/business/services/PayrollAuditService.ts: constructor(private readonly prisma: PrismaService) and calls this.prisma.payrollAudit.create(...) and this.prisma.payrollAudit.findMany(...) directly
src/business/services/PayrollAuditService.ts: log() builds the persistence id `${Date.now()}-${subject}` and the 'at: new Date()' column inline, which is storage work a repository would normally own
src/business/services/PayrollAuditService.ts: export interface AuditLine is defined in the services folder instead of under src/business/model like Timesheet/Payslip
parsedVerdict.reasoning: Both files cover payroll: timesheets and payslips in one, the payroll audit trail in the other. That is cohesive enough. The abstraction is not consistent, though. PayrollService reaches persistence through repositories (EmployeeRepository, TimesheetRepository) and builds domain model objects (Employee, Timesheet, Payslip). PayrollAuditService skips that and works on the raw Prisma client (prisma.payrollAudit.create/findMany). It also builds the storage id itself (`${Date.now()}-${subject}`), sets the 'at' timestamp, and defines its own read type, AuditLine, in the service file instead of using a model. So within this one module, the two services use different boundaries to reach persistence, and one of them skips the repository abstraction the module otherwise uses. This judges the inconsistent abstraction, not which layers may import which.

violations.message: Skips the module's repository abstraction: PayrollAuditService uses PrismaService directly (prisma.payrollAudit.create/findMany) and builds the record id and timestamp inline, while PayrollService goes only through EmployeeRepository/TimesheetRepository and domain models. The two services use different persistence boundaries.
